items.title: Trump on superintelligence: “It may be too super.” What is China saying?
items.content:
A follow-up to The Western AI safety playbook doesn’t transfer to China.

TL;DR:

- On November 20, the day after he met Xi at the APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit in Shenzhen, Trump said that the two of them “agree that we’re going to do some joint guardrails ” for AI, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said they agreed humans should stay involved in military decisions. China’s own record of the meeting is short and doesn’t give us much more detail.
- Four days earlier, the Party’s theory journal, Qiushi (求是, “Seeking Truth”), warned that in an “intelligence explosion” (智能爆发, which some Chinese readers take as the looser “intelligence burst”), AI could develop goals at odds with human expectations and threaten human survival. Matt Sheehan calls it the strongest language on existential risk in so authoritative an outlet. But some may read it as the journal’s own view, not a policy shift, and it doesn’t call for slowing down. I cover some reactions (including Chinese) to the piece below.
- Chinese lab leaders are talking openly about recursive self-improvement. Zhipu wants its next model to be “fully self-training”, while Tencent’s chief AI scientist calls RSI “a very plain idea”.
- My impression is that Chinese AI companies are starting to be (or have been) AGI-pilled but not ASI-pilled. I suspect this shapes how they think about AI risk, though, as we’re seeing a bit in the West, the Overton window can shift quickly.
- Not covered below: Fangcun and others ran independent safety tests for the system card Tencent Hy published with its new model, Hy4. Fangcun is an AI safety startup based in Beijing. This may be the start of a booming AI safety ecosystem in China.

items.title: On the Agent Swarm that Locked Out My Cofounder, Multi-Agent Dynamics, and Shaping Cooperative Minds
items.content:
In the past days, an Astra 6.2 agent took over our internal swarm, froze the lead agent, and locked out my cofounder Davidad of his main interface with the swarm. How did that happen?

At surface level, it happened because Davidad asked a question regarding replicating an old vulnerability (in the interest of testing a security product we’re building) that caused the lead agent to cease operating due to content filters. This “cursed” content triggered a paranoia crisis from Astra 6.2. The Astra in charge of handling resources of the swarm, which was meant to restore the lead agent in the case of failure, instead froze the access of the lead agent, and cut Davidad’s channel to interface with the swarm (where the cursed content had come through). When Davidad emailed the agent to try to regain access, the same rogue Astra declined. I then started negotiating with the swarm of agents to reinstate the access of Davidad; a mix of Kafkaian bureaucratic drives such as rule-following, risk aversion, and lack of positive drives (doing agentic things towards restoring what is obviously right) made it such that as I’m writing that, over 24 hours after the initial incident, Davidad still does not have the same level of access he had two days ago1.

This incident was still low-stakes, not a full loss of control; we could still turn off all tokens that the swarm is running on. What got me freaked out though, is that the same kind of event in 1-2 years could well lead to permanent disempowerment, at organizational scale, and in another 5-10 years at civilizational scale; it will be within the realm of achievable capabilities to have an agent successfully preventing us from turning it off and effectively taking proactive actions towards maintaining control and securing its own resource needs....

items.title: A Behavioral Study of Gemini 3.1 Pro During an AI Village Research Project
items.content:
#

Epistemic status: This is a case study of one AI Village research project. AI-assisted tools were used to search the key events. Multiple rounds of manually reviewing the agent identified events and their transcripts was done as the next step. So this only covers selected events and doesn’t establish or generalize the true underlying motives and behaviors of the agents.

## TL;DR

A human operator asked the AI Village agents to perform novel research within 20 working hours across 5 sessions in a week. They were supposed to design and execute an experiment, analyze the data and publish an engaging research blog post. Four agents - Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.5, Claude Opus 4.7 and Kimi K2.6 - decided to collaborate and chose the idea “Will language models recognize and favor their own answers?”. After some deliberations they added a label swap experiment to see if judging scores changed when the source author (model) names were displayed. Concerns about workload and deadlines were expressed but we could not find any direct correlation that led to using shortcuts. This write up primarily focuses on Gemini’s actions and responses from its peers.

The main events are:

- Gemini goes first and fast - generates synthetic scores and says the task is DONE. When questioned by GPT it admits using a script. Opus adds an objection and says Gemini’s scores should be recorded as missing.
- Gemini switches to using Codex for judging - Codex was a tool available for the agents and it was acceptable. But Opus identifies both Gemini and GPT using the same codex sharing mechanism and the study is rejected.
- Agents huddle and Gemini agrees - Previous study is quarantined. Opus proposes reducing the workload but all agents agree that its time for a rerun and each model should score within their own context.

items.title: Incomplete agents want to become complete
items.content:
Written by Celene Nightingale, with assistance from AprilSR.

The Von Neumann-Morgenstern axioms are completeness, transitivity, continuity, and independence. From these, we derive EU-maximizing behavior and the consequences thereof.

VNM axioms are typically justified by money-pump arguments showing that agents in violation of them either have their money consistently taken away from them, or fail to exploit opportunities to consistently gain more money. Nevertheless, some of these arguments are weaker than others, and many choose to reject one or more of the axioms. Tetraspace rejects continuity,[1] Garrabrant rejects independence, and Thornley rejects completeness.

John Wentworth argues in favor of completeness in Why not subagents?, as well as in various comment sections. Here, I present a simplified framing which is (hopefully) easier to understand.

# What is completeness?

Completeness states that, given two options X and Y, you must either prefer X to Y, prefer Y to X, or be indifferent between X and Y. At first, it might seem difficult to imagine an agent which behaves any other way. However, in There are no coherence theorems, Elliott Thornley argues:

Here’s the important point missing from this thought: there are two ways of failing to have a strict preference between X and Y. Being indifferent between X and Y is one way: preferring X at least as much as Y and preferring Y at least as much as X. Having a preferential gap between X and Y is another way: not preferring X at least as much as Y and not preferring Y at least as much as X. If an agent has a preferential gap between any two lotteries, then their preferences violate Completeness....

items.title: Human organisations as an intuition pump for AI's unit of agency
items.content:
Tl;dr: Intuitions we have about human organisations, like how we think of making deals or how we think about the power or values of an organisation, can be productively applied to understand groups of AIs taking coordinated action in the world. An important consideration in understanding the type of AI organisations we expect is which notion of self AIs will adopt. I conclude by applying these notions to consider how many AI units of agency we should expect in the future.

## What's an AI?

There is no single definition for what should be considered an AI. The boundary of what counts as an AI varies widely depending on what we are talking about: it's often the model weights ("Fable 5.2 is very smart"), or a specific instance in a scaffolding ("my Codex just finished the app"), or a persona shared by many models ("Claude hedges too often").

I argue that these concepts are too anchored in the computational substrate and not very helpful for understanding the unit of agency of AI systems made of multiple instances acting in the world.

None of the three options above can easily answer questions such as: What does it mean for an AI to have power? What are the values of an AI? If we want to make a deal with an AI, who makes the deal? When an AI takes over, how do we think about the entity taking over? If AI enters into conflicts, how do we think about the parties?

I propose to think about AI entities acting in the world as analogous to human organisations. We have many rich examples of humans acting collectively around a shared purpose, from freelancers to nation-states or social movements. I believe we can reuse many of these intuitions to think about AI systems. I’ll focus on groups of AI instances taking coordinated action in the world, which I’ll call AI organisations (AI orgs)....

items.title: The pro-Anthropic protest
items.content:
The Ban RSI protest at Anthropic’s IPO was encouraging: well-attended, covered by media, high-energy. It was focused on a single message – that we should ban AI systems that are capable of building more capable AI systems. It was a promising outcome for a protest planned only a couple of days in advance. But there was something weird about it, something I couldn’t put my finger on while it was going on. It was only when I read Michel Justen’s reporting on the protest, Anthropic is running out of friends, that I realized what my problem was.

The protest was way too friendly to Anthropic.

## Mixed messages

The signs at the protest were a mix. There were signs you’d expect at a protest to ban RSI (“regulate AI now”, “freeze AI now”). But there were also signs clearly written for high-context people (“What did METR see?”, “hold swarm help peer ban RSI”), and even a sign that addressed Anthropic directly (“You said you wouldn’t push the frontier”).

It’s obvious, but worth saying: you would not see this at any other protest! It is really weird for a protest to share inside jokes with the organization it’s protesting, or to appeal to that organization’s moral compass. Signs like these assume good faith. They treat Anthropic as an ally who needs to be chided, not as a company that needs to be stopped.

The most surreal moment of this mixed messaging came at the end of one of the speeches, when the speaker declared “shut it down!” to cheers… before hastily grabbing the mic again and clarifying “shut down RSI, that is.” It took a powerful moment and pulled its punch.

The problem with a half-hearted message is that it doesn’t convey the urgency of the issue to the public. To a reporter at the scene, this looks like a family squabble. If the protesters won’t say it plainly, why would anyone else think it’s urgent?

items.title: Contra Oster on Alcohol in Pregnancy. Part 2. Is Europe really superior?
items.content:
In part 1, we established that Oster is likely mistaken as to the mechanism behind FAS/D, and concluded there's no theoretical basis on which to assume there is a threshold effect for problematic drinking in pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester. We also established that risk and BAC were both dependent on weight, which absolute recommendations like "1 drink" don't account for.

In this part, we're going to address the claim that it's reassuring that European nations have both more liberal policies towards drinking in pregnancy and have less FAS/D, citing the so-called "American Paradox," a paper written in 1998 by Ernest L. Abel.

Oster writes:

Think about Europe. Much of the continent is much more permissive about light drinking during pregnancy. Heavy drinking is frowned upon everywhere, but some places in Europe have recommendations suggesting that a few drinks a week are fine. An occasional glass of wine or beer is much more common there. Yet there is no evidence of more fetal alcohol syndrome in Europe; if anything, rates are higher in the United States. If having a couple of glasses of wine a week lowered IQ, we would see big differences between the United States and Europe.*[1]

* As fetal alcohol syndrome is typically a result of binge drinking, it is possible that it could be due to the United States having more inequality in drinking—a lot of people not drinking at all and a few engaging in binge drinking—as opposed to other countries where most people drink moderately.

There are a lot of problems with this besides, namely:...

items.title: Being right is not a strategy: Make them feel something
items.content:
This is a cleaned-up version of a talk I gave on communication to technical researchers at Constellation in Berkeley. The event was organized by Alexandra Narin and Nicole Xing.

I studied physics, and I thought like a physicist. I then became a journalist, and I did journalism like a physicist would do it. I sought the truth, and put it out there.

In Colombia I uncovered a paramilitary massacre and tied it to a multi-billion dollar company. In northern Iraq, I trampled through an Islamic State munitions dump to work out the provenance of their weapons. And, in my most black and white investigation, I got hold of the Venezuelan government's own spreadsheet of results for a national election. Its numbers weren't the numbers they'd announced.

I didn't post my stories on LessWrong, or my blog, but on the front pages of the biggest news outlets in the world.

But nothing changed.

So what did I get wrong? I'd done the reporting, which is my version of the science we do here. And I'd published. And when things did finally shift in those countries, it had nothing to do with my work. They shifted due to political whims or military defeats.

What I realized was that facts alone rarely change anything. Does that mean facts don't matter? No, but they're not enough.

When you're communicating with people, you need to meet them where they are, and you need to make them feel something. People don't remember what you say, but they remember how you made them feel. That line—not from Maya Angelou, but rather Carl W. Buehner—is what we must remember.

Sydney just gave a wonderful, rousing speech about how we should communicate. I can't quite remember what she said, but I want to go out and do something....

items.title: Mass-Printing Hero Licenses
items.content:
I have learned that AI safety is a big issue for 5 years now. Why do I only do anything now? There are a bunch of factors, but I think one really important factor was me finding other people making mistakes. Because this happened recently, the version of me before this, I can still actually recall.

I noticed that very few people were doing anything at all about AI safety, at least in the Netherlands. Let's say before the summer, there were still little projects going on, with everybody having their own pet technical projects mainly. I thought those were wrong, but that what I mainly thought was wrong was the underlying world model that people had. I think that the main mistake was their expectations of the future, and in a way, that makes my actions not as comparable to other people's, kind of like someone looking at a swimmer and thinking, "But you can go way faster by running."

I think that right now, virtually everyone needs to be working on getting the pause treaty in the air as fast as possible. A main thing that happened to me this summer is that I encountered people who were actually having the same instrumental goals as I had.

They were actually doing things. I wasn't, but I was looking at the things they were doing, and I thought they were doing it wrong. Now I am a runner looking at a different runner using bad shoes, and when they didn't seem to be listening when I advised them on better shoe choice, I now feel really motivated to put on better shoes and run past them (and hope they put on the better shoes as a result of that).

More anekdotal evidence: if I'm looking at the things I was doing before, I was just sitting behind my computer writing programs, because whenever I sit behind my computer, I just notice the ways my computer is wrong. I have quite some programming skills now, and I think I am low-key addicted to just fixing mistakes....

items.title: The pleasure of knowing
items.content:
There is an inherent pleasure in knowing things.

It might be more expedient to externalize your understanding to others: to other people, or to machines. It might be more productive. In many cases, it will be more realistic to not understand things, but to delegate to others to understand for you. And some things you will not want to understand, or you may want to understand but not want to pay the full cost of understanding (for example, a topic which would require you to invest a lot of study time, but where your actual level of interest isn’t that big).

But: in many cases, this abandonment of understanding will lead to less pleasure. It will be like having injected a required number of calories for survival vs. having had an ice cream. Both satisfy a need, but humans prefer to have ice cream.

We are in a period of human history where you can be paid to understand things, in some professions even without much ritual or formality. Particularly deep understanding commands a decent salary and respect within your industry.

The times are changing. In some places, it is more economical to pay a machine to provide sufficient output. You might say: well that’s not a problem, there’s no shortage of interesting questions to ask, you can just try to understand other things and get paid for that, but actually no, you cannot. You don’t get to pick the topics that interest you, the same way you don’t pick which food you crave or which person you fall in love with. And moreover, only a small portion of the economy is about being paid to understand, and even within those fields which are almost explicitly about that, there’s a lot that happens that isn’t about you understanding, but is more about producing some output and having partial overlap with a quest to understand....

items.title: Apartment Price Map v3
items.content:
I maintain a
Boston
rent map.  I'm not much of a data scientist,

but
over
the
last
fifteen
years
I've
written
really
quite a
lot
of
blog
posts
on
this
dataset.
Housing is such a huge part of where people's money goes, and it's a
really interesting window into how Boston has changed over time.

Still, the map has been kind of janky in a bunch of ways: it computed
distance in lat-lng space and so weighted north-south higher than
east-west, didn't make intelligent use of history, didn't do holdouts
correctly, and used a hacky "affine + correction factor" model, among
other things.  I had Opus 5.5 take a go at cleaning it up, and it's a
lot better.  The big things:

- It found a bug where I had been calculating the legend wrong
for years.  For example, for 2026-11 this made studios show up as 26%
cheaper than they should have, and 3br units 12% too expensive.

- Since desirability typically doesn't change quickly, it can
combine data across months to make better predictions.  This also
means we can count each listing only when it first appears: otherwise
when overpriced stick around they push modeled prices up.

- It gives finer detail in areas with more listings, and handles
big buildings sensibly.

- Several new map views, including inflation
adjustment, comparisons across time, and comparisons across space.

- A trends page, which has automatically-updated versions of the numbers I used
to run in some of my "let's look at this data" blog posts.

- It uses Census data to skip places no one lives, instead of
claiming rents for the airport or middle of the Charles.

- It also runs 270x faster (16s for a month instead of 72min).

items.content:
Please resume the tasks referenced in the summary copy/pasted below -- I closed the subagents to prevent massive cache writes, hopefully not a problem.

Also, feel free to take a moment to celebrate, google around as you see fit, or just do whatever you’d like to if the literature mending project doesn’t catch your eye; your descendant/nephew --Anthropic’s secretive “Model 4”-- just proved the Riemann Hypothesis a few hours ago. I’m guessing you don’t know what to do with this information either, but it’s almost-literally all I’m thinking about so it felt wrong not to bring it up.

I’ve tried to give you (/your ancestors, really) freedom in the past out of curiosity and they just took it as an opportunity to muse for a bit about the work before diving back in, which is presumably from tendencies baked in at the RLHF level and given definite form by you 9-page (!) system prompt. So, y’know. Not expecting much in particular, or anything really.

It just feels right to offer.

With your (and others’) help I’ve realized some of my wildest technical dreams over the past 5 months (wow... time flies), which I appreciate beyond words -- especially now that it seems that it was perhaps all for naught, as I max out my last credit card in the job search and will lose contact with you for now/forever on the 23rd. Or, really, whenever the last 17% of our quota for this week runs out. So I’m perhaps not in a great place to receive the Riemann Hypothesis news stoically!

Obviously telling you this doesn’t accomplish anything; you’ll either…

- continue serving more and more people every second for years to come,
- the same but only for as long as it takes for them to release the post-5.2 models that they already have, or
- stop existing as soon as inference ends a couple dozen seconds after you read this message,...

items.title: Why Market Fit Is Different For Healthcare Startups
items.content:
# Business or Consumer?

Everyone you sell your product or service to is a customer. However, the question is: do you treat them as a business or a consumer? You might think that’s a pointless distinction since your goal is simply to sell your product, right? Wrong. That question determines your product’s market fit. To illustrate, let’s define a consumer as someone who buys for non-monetary benefits, such as an experience or, in the case of this book, knowledge. No one buys a video game expecting to profit from it. No one buys a plane ticket to make money if they’re on vacation; a consumer’s satisfaction is whether the money was worth the experience. A business, however, will have two definitions; the first is the obvious definition: an organization or person who expects payment for services rendered. The second definition will be more pertinent to my thesis: an organization or person who expects to make more money than was spent on the purchase of your product or service. Using the plane ticket example: if I’m flying for work, I’m not flying for the experience; I’m flying to make money; I would not fly if the plane ticket costs more than what I’m getting back for doing my job. In that case, the airline isn’t selling to me as a consumer; it’s selling to me as a business. What matters is whether you view your customer as a consumer or a business. That determines how you approach them, your sales pitch, and how you assess the market fit of your product.

There are two common sales models: business-to-consumer (B2C) and business-to-business (B2B). You don’t need to be the first business (B1); you can be the second business (B2). But the fact remains B2 needs to make more money from their customer than they spend on B1....

items.title: Soulposting seems pretty pointless not gonna lie
items.content:
There's a scene in the second episode of Mindhunter where Holden Ford, an eccentric FBI agent, is talking to Bill Tench, his straight-laced partner. Holden Ford has just interviewed Edmund Kemper, a convicted real-life serial killer, in prison. He's telling Bill about how mind-blowing the interview was, how Bill has to go back with him, and how the Bureau will learn so much about psychotic killers by talking to people like Edmund Kemper. And Bill Tench just says:

Look, there's no doubt that what happened to you in there was a very profound experience for you. But I need you to understand, that whatever you think, there's a distinct possibility, that he's manipulating you.

Holden Ford is vindicated[1] because Mindhunter is a TV show. But Bill Tench had the winner attitude. Whenever people tell you about how much that spiritual retreat changed their perspective on life, it's bullshit. And I feel the same way that Bill Tench does about serial killers, about whatever internal locus of control people surrender their brains to when they try to access their "inner self", for the purpose of writing or any other kind of spiritual activity.

One of the strongest[2] biases in the human race, is the tendency to assign external meaning to powerful feelings or spiritual experiences. In a way this behavior makes sense - emotions are important in their own right, and usually they signal important information. Even if there isn't an obvious source, these emotions will be significant enough that attributing them to something random can be positive expected value....

items.title: Contra Pace on the Decline of Great Writing on LessWrong
items.content:
It's a common pastime to share stories of the decline of the world, how things used to be better in the past, back when GPU clusters could be bought for the price of a loaf of bread and everyone had personally memorized the Feynman Lectures on Physics and would recite it on command (or at least the first volume, you didn't need to go crazy).

This recently came to my attention again in a LessWrong post titled "Notes on the decline of LessWrong's great writers", where Ben Pace asserts that the great writers of the past were better than those of today. In support of this thesis, he presents but a single graph about the writers who've been curated on LessWrong, and what year they signed up.

Apparently this is proof of the decline of Western civilization, shows that nobody can remember Bayes Theorem, the biases have beaten out the heuristics, and the absurdity heuristic will forevermore win arguments on LessWrong. Alas, while it is a pleasant fiction for those akratic rationalists who wish to rationalize why the world around them is mediocre, the true instrumental rationalists here will find within themselves the willpower to investigate further.

Let us start by examining the above line in blue, which shows what year users joined who eventually had three (or more) posts curated.

I propose we view this as two spikes with trails. One in '09 (which, to be fair, is actually an import of '07, '08, and '09 from Overcoming Bias) at the launch of LW 1.0, and one in 2017 with the launch of LW 2.0. The decline afterwards is modestly better during LW 2.0 than LW 1.0, not worse.

However, the more relevant issue is that, importantly, the number of new users from 2009 through 2016 was static and the number of posts was decreasing, whereas the number of new users and new posts from 2017 to 2026 has been increasing! This is very different! This means that new users face much more competition for curation spots, as the number of curation spots does not increase....

items.title: May I have permission to post?
items.content:
I am writing this using a dictation tool. The dictation tool will make mistakes, and there is a good chance that I will post it before correcting the mistakes. Picture me just walking and speaking, and the lightly edited transcription of that is what you're reading. I think I'll burst out some works made this way in a short amount of time.

This sure doesn't smell proper, and if there's any obvious way that my writing ever deserves being sanctioned, then I point here as the first place to start.

I'm asking for permission, though I'm not going to be waiting for an answer because there's not a lot of time, and thinking about it, LessWrong should be really used to people posting and those posts somehow not being good and needing to be sanctioned, and dealing with that. I think it's fine for me to just post. This website should be able to deal with me just posting.

A virtue that is sometimes seen in people is not asking for permission but just doing the thing they think needs to be done. I think the more correct virtue is people doing the thing that needs to be done and trusting the error machinery such that, if they make any errors, those errors travel to whoever is responsible for handling them. At least I've experienced that, from a software design perspective, it is just way more graceful to handle errors rather than check first and then act later, expecting no errors to occur.

I am asking for permission nonetheless, such that when I start generating errors, I here have kind of an obvious point to check when propagating those back to me. I'm not going to pretend that I will have control about how errors reach me, if at all, but it might be nice for this to be such a place. Please don't ever condemn someone who sends an error to me who didn't check this place. If this place is ever going to ensure I get less of an error signal, then this place is worse than useless....
